newsitem.title: LATVIA: BALTICS-WORLD BANK SEES RUSSIAN CRUDE EXPORT GROWTH.
newsitem.headline: BALTICS-WORLD BANK SEES RUSSIAN CRUDE EXPORT GROWTH.

text.p: The World Bank said on Wednesday that Russian crude oil transit through the port of Ventspils could increase substantially, provided it adds capacity and Russia does not opt for other routes.

"There is a shortfall of transit capacity compared to potential Russian export (growth), which could cheaply be added in Latvia's Ventspils and Novorossiysk on the Black sea," Lars Jeurling, head of the World Bank's Baltic mission, told a Baltic transit conference.
The Bank said it sees Russian crude oil shipments outside of the former Soviet Union of 130 million tonnes in the year 2000 and 165 million tonnes in the year 2005 against 105 million in 1995.
Caspian transit oil could add 10 to 20 percent to these numbers, Jeurling told the conference.
"Ventspils and Novorossiysk are the least costly options for supplying additional capacity (for the apparent shortfall)," Jeurlings said.
The shortfall in 2005 could be 34 to 82 million tonnes, Jeurling added.
There is no certainty that this will benefit the Baltic countries as there are other pipeline and port possibilities, he said.
"The competition is still there despite the need for additional capacity," Jeurling said.
"A pipeline could be extended through Austria to reopen the Adria line through the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary," Jeurling said.
"Russia also has plans for oil facilities in the St. Petersburg area Primorsk, which, if implemented, would take care of the need for increased oil shipping facilities for a long time," he said.
A World Bank study indicates that there is sufficient capacity in Russia to handle the increased volumes of its exports and imports at least through the year 2005 except for crude oil.
